          "text": "# Canopus, the Southern Lantern\n\n*An A-type bright giant rides low over northern horizons\u2014and burns high in the south. Here\u2019s how to find it, and what its light reveals.*\n\nCanopus is a star with two very different views. From much of the Southern Hemisphere, it climbs high and commands attention; from farther north, it skims the horizon, a bright point glimpsed through the thickest layer of our atmosphere. Either way, it rewards a clear view south.\n\nLook for it in Carina, the Keel, whose stars belong to the southern sky. Canopus is catalogued as Alpha Carinae, and its reported visual magnitude is \u20130.74: unmistakably bright to the naked eye. It is not a nearby lamp, though. Its measured parallax is 10.55 milliarcseconds, placing it roughly 310 light-years away. That distance is an estimate calculated from the parallax listed in SIMBAD. [SIMBAD: Canopus / HIP 30438](https://simbad.cds.unistra.fr/simbad/sim-id?Ident=HIP%2030438)\n\nThe same catalogue gives Canopus a spectral type of A9 II. The \u201cA\u201d identifies a hot, white star; \u201cII\u201d marks its luminosity class as a bright giant. Its apparent brilliance is a combination of intrinsic luminosity and distance\u2014not simply a sign that it sits close to Earth. A star\u2019s spectrum, read from the light it emits, helps astronomers classify its temperature and evolutionary state.\n\nFor observers, the most important number may be the star\u2019s declination: about 52 degrees 42 minutes south. That puts a limit on where it can be seen. North of roughly 37\u00b0 north latitude, Canopus never rises above the geometric horizon. Near that boundary, even a place where it technically clears the horizon may offer a poor view: haze, buildings, trees and the thick air near the horizon can dim or hide it.\n\nIf you\u2019re observing from a more northerly site where Canopus does rise, choose a spot with an unobstructed southern horizon.
